https://www.politico.eu/article/hackers-.text: BRUSSELS — Foreign governments have been trying to hack the messaging accounts of high-ranking European Union officials, the bloc’s cyber defense unit said in an internal presentation obtained by POLITICO. The presentation, given to officials from EU national governments in July, lists “account takeover targeting high-ranking officials” as one of the top threats facing the bloc this year. The presentation is the first official acknowledgment that EU officials were targeted by cyberattacks through messaging apps, after several national cyber agencies flagged an ongoing campaign linked to Russian threat groups earlier this year. The presentation is also the first reported instance in which an EU authority formally links such attacks to a foreign government. Advertisement Advertisement The officials were the targets of so-called “state-sponsored spearphishing,” the presentation said, a term for state-backed, targeted and bespoke campaigns to get specific people to click on dodgy links or open malicious attachments. Hackers used "social engineering techniques" to trick EU officials, crafting personalized messages that were more likely to get targets to take the bait. Earlier this year, POLITICO first reported that the European Commission told some of its most senior officials to shut down a Signal group over hacking fears. It came at the same time as a series of warnings by national cyber authorities telling governments to move away from commercial messaging apps like WhatsApp and Signal for official business. In March, at least five national cyber and intelligence agencies publicly warned about ongoing hacking campaigns on Signal and WhatsApp. Dutch intelligence services specifically pinned this on Russia, and Germany warned that hackers were targeting “high-ranking individuals in politics, the military, and diplomacy, as well as investigative journalists.” The agencies warned then that hackers were posing as a fake Signal support chatbot to persuade users to share their codes, allowing them to take over an account to read incoming communications and group chats. EU cybersecurity officials said in the presentation that the bloc's institutions had faced eight "significant incidents" so far this year. One key challenge, they flagged, is that the different EU institutions still use different technical cybersecurity solutions and lack a common solution to exchange sensitive and classified documents. The European Commission declined to give details on internal security practices in response to POLITICO's questions on the presentation. WhatsApp and Signal did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/gov.text: The Budapest Times Government declassifies secret decrees revealing how public billions flowed to Orbán-era think tanks The government has published the first batch of so-called "three-thousand" government decrees — classified until now — issued over the past 16 years, government communications announced to MTI on Wednesday. The "first package" concerns Századvég, showing what government decisions and commissions formed the basis for channelling public funds to the organisation, and through what arrangements. The documents will make visible to everyone what decisions the Orbán government kept from the public, and how the “state public-money pump” operated over the past decade and a half, the statement said. According to the communiqué, the government is now making public thirteen decisions concerning research and studies financed from public funds, but the process will continue with the presentation of around one hundred decisions in total. The statement explained that the original purpose of “three-thousand government decrees” is to prevent government decisions containing genuinely sensitive information — such as matters related to national security or national defence — from becoming public. The current review, however, shows that over the past 16 years this instrument was also used to conceal matters for which maintaining secrecy can no longer be justified, it added. The statement stressed that the Prime Minister’s Office is reviewing the three-thousand government decrees of the past 16 years and, wherever the statutory conditions for maintaining the classification no longer apply, will revoke it. Genuine state secrets must continue to be protected, but the use of public funds cannot in itself justify classifying data and excluding the public, they stated. In these resolutions, the Orbán governments typically decided to commission public opinion research, media research, media analysis, and consultancy services; a total of approximately 65 billion forints was set aside for research through these decisions, they added. According to the statement, the decisions include ordering media impact research in Central Europe, Albania, and the Baltic states, as well as ordering representative public opinion polling covering the entire population of the European Union and the populations of Balkan countries. They emphasised that government resolutions are not contracts in themselves, and that in parallel with the review of the resolutions, the Prime Minister’s Office is also reviewing the performance certificates of the contracts concluded, in order to determine whether public funds were managed with due care in every case. The government is also examining the studies and analyses produced under the contracts, in order to determine whether criminal or other liability exists, they wrote. They stated that the publication of the documents is a further step in uncovering how the Orbán system operated: what decisions were made, to which actors, and for what purposes public funds were channelled in a manner whose details were kept from the Hungarian people for years or even decades. Regarding the first “package,” they stated: under the governments after 2010, Századvég’s role and state funding grew markedly. The group conducted opinion polls, political and policy analyses, and strategic consulting for the state, while receiving government contracts worth billions year after year, they added. Századvég thus became, funded by public money, one of the central analytical and advisory bodies supporting the Orbán government’s policies. The first package of the so-called “three-thousand” government decrees — previously classified and now made public — also offers insight into the workings of this system: it shows what government decisions and contracts, and through what arrangements, public money could flow to Századvég. The documents thus make visible part of the decision-making mechanism behind the payments already known to date. The documents are available at https://kormany.hu/titkositott-kormanyhatarozatok, the statement reads. Bálint Ruff, the head of the Prime Minister’s Office, stated in an early September interview given to Telex that the government has so far filed complaints in cases totalling two thousand billion forints. In a video interview published last Wednesday, Bálint Ruff said that a review of Századvég is underway — an organisation that received between 20 and 30 billion forints in public funds over the past ten years for writing studies and conducting research — and indicated that a criminal complaint will also be filed in this matter. The minister recalled that complaints have already been filed in connection with Observer, which carried out media monitoring for “horrendous” sums, as well as against the Kommentár Foundation, for which “properties were purchased for twenty billion.” He added that his colleagues are “already adding up” the amounts paid to the Nézőpont Institute. The Hungarian state paid 10 to 20 billion forints for something that ChatGPT can produce in 0.1 seconds, he stated, adding that within a few weeks a public procurement tender will be issued for polling tasks, and once it has been assessed, every study commissioned by the Hungarian state will be made public. In response to a question about criminal liability, he indicated that it is for the investigating authority to decide. Every contract was signed by someone, he said — “the ones worth three thousand, for example, by the prime minister of the time.” He noted, however, that filing a complaint takes little time, whereas a police investigation takes considerably longer. https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/10/03/b.text: BATANGAS CITY — The 11-crew members at the Analog Habitat Waypoint (Anahaw) have successfully completed a 24-hour simulation at a facility in Batangas State University (BatStateU) practicing as astronauts under severe isolation, communication lag, and physical limits of a lunar base. The completed simulation forms part of a broader push by the Philippine Space Agency (PhilSA) to build a regional hub for analog astronaut missions. Ahead of the deployment, four experienced Filipino analog astronauts met with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at Malacañan Palace to outline future spaceflight initiatives.The primary crew members lived and worked inside the simulated environment, navigating operational isolation and resource limitations. Five additional team members staffed mission control under the Space Infrastructure Management and Deployment Division, monitoring operations, managing procurement and training protocols, and responding to simulated emergency scenarios.Anahaw followed a six-part preparatory lecture series held from April to June 2026, designed to train personnel in analog habitat architecture, extravehicular suits, life support infrastructure, and flight-readiness protocols.Kristine Jane Atienza, the first Filipina analog astronaut, served as a key resource person and lead lecturer for the series. Drawing from her background as a nutrition specialist and medical officer at the Hawaiʻi Space Exploration Analog and Simulation habitat on Mauna Loa, she prepared the Batangas habitat for the operational realities of off-world life while putting a spotlight on a critical discipline: space food engineering.Atienza has spent years demonstrating that survival rations in isolated, confined environments must be treated simultaneously as medicine, logistics, and psychology.“Feeding an astronaut is far more complex than stowing freeze-dried camping rations in a locker,” Atienza told The Manila Times. “Beyond Earth’s atmosphere, extreme environments disrupt human physiology. Microgravity drives bodily fluids upward toward the head, causing chronic nasal congestion similar to a severe head cold.” The fluid shift blunts olfactory and taste receptors, causing standard meals to taste like damp cardboard. Simultaneously, cosmic radiation, accelerated muscle atrophy, and rapid bone calcium loss require precise formulas packed with potassium and bioavailable protein, while keeping sodium and iron strictly controlled.These insights helped shape how crew health is viewed inside the Batangas habitat, where preparation routines faced rigid mass and energy constraints. Boiling water draws heavily on microgrid power reserves, requiring recipes optimized for passive rehydration.“Crumbly dry goods are strictly out of the question because loose specks foul sensitive environmental air scrubbers and irritate crew eyes,” Atienza stressed. “Waste is equally uncompromising; packaging cannot simply be tossed into a dustbin when every cubic centimeter of discarded plastic consumes vital habitat volume.” To combat menu fatigue—a major cause of declining cognitive clarity and crew morale during longduration confinement—Atienza champions using Southeast Asian food chemistry. Rather than adding excess salt, sour bases from calamansi and tamarind, garlic-heavy aromatics, and the naturally protective vinegar reductions of traditional adobo offer strong flavors that pierce sensory dullness.Her ongoing research with the Philippine Nuclear Research Institute (PNRI) and the University of the Philippines Diliman (UPD) explores using gamma irradiation to sterilize traditional staples, such as Philippine dried mangoes and shelf-stable meat dishes, ensuring long-term shelf stability without degrading delicate vitamins or protein texture.Mission leaders are currently parsing data gathered from the 24-hour run to evaluate how Filipino crews handle isolation, monotony, and resource rationing, with an emphasis on how cultural adaptability and communal cooperation, or bayanihan, function under high stress.“The Analog Habitat Waypoint reminds us that our journey into space begins long before we leave the ground,” said PhilSA Acting Director General Gay Jane P.Perez, Ph.D. “It begins with curiosity, science and preparation, and people who are willing to go first. You chose to step into this habitat, and what you have learned here can now help others take the next step.” PhilSA has already announced the Anahaw 2.0 expansion across regional campuses, alongside a two-week, all-Filipino professional mission abroad in 2027 targeting facilities such as the LunAres Research Station in Poland or the Mars Desert Research Station in Utah.The initiative lays the programmatic groundwork for PhilSA’s broader roadmap to qualify an astronaut candidate by 2029.
